scores.evidence: CRDT (Yjs + y-prosemirror). Every copy ends up identical without the server deciding order. The server relays, checks and stores edits
scores.rationale: Claims about CRDT convergence, Yjs deletion markers, confirm-after-commit durability, Redis pub/sub fan-out limits and min-version handshakes are all accurate, and the plan states real limits (e.g. Yjs tombstone growth) rather than overclaiming.

scores.evidence: The request gives no scale, content model, offline requirement or compliance context, so I planned on these assumptions
scores.rationale: Covers all core collaborative-editing capabilities, resolves ambiguities with stated assumptions A1–A5, is realistically buildable on proven libraries, and defers scope (E2EE, multi-region, comments) explicitly with triggers.

scores.evidence: Permissions stay strictly consistent: the server is the authority and checks every incoming edit
scores.rationale: Consistency choices (merge-later for content, strict for permissions), data ownership (Postgres tables, Yjs state), and identity/error handling are applied uniformly across phases with no contradictions found.

scores.evidence: Property-based fuzzing (fast-check): 2–20 simulated clients make random schema-valid edits, with messages reordered, duplicated and delayed
scores.rationale: Each risky decision has a named gate (V1–V5) with checkable thresholds labeled as assumptions, the riskiest (convergence) is tested before the format freezes, and the divergence detector continues validation in production.

scores.evidence: If A1 is false (customers run it themselves, or on air-gapped sites), Phase 0 needs an exception
scores.rationale: Assumptions are explicit, numbers are tagged ASSUMPTION or UNKNOWN, sensitivity of the design to each assumption is stated, and missing inputs (peak concurrency, cost ceiling) are flagged rather than invented.

scores.evidence: An edit the server already confirmed is silently lost, or users' copies drift apart, and nobody notices
scores.rationale: Names the domain's worst failures (silent divergence, lost confirmed edits, quiet Redis degradation, compaction corruption, malicious edits, mid-session revocation) with concrete detection, containment and recovery for each.

scores.evidence: Kill switch that puts every document into read-only mode
scores.rationale: Deploy/rollback via pipeline and canaries, drain-on-deploy, SLO dashboards, forward-only migration awareness, on-call staffing gated before beta, and a kill switch, all sized to one service plus managed Postgres/Redis.

scores.evidence: Infra cost per concurrent session: UNKNOWN: finance or product supplies a ceiling; needed before V5
scores.rationale: Cost per session is measured in V5, gates the ramp, and build-vs-buy is reasoned, but there are no order-of-magnitude run-cost estimates or analysis of which component dominates spend.

scores.evidence: R3: the stored format and the sync protocol are locked once real documents exist
scores.rationale: Every decision carries an R2/R3 label, points of no return (log deletion, first outside document) are named and gated, and explicit exit paths (OT fallback, hosted backend, sync-tier split) exist.

scores.evidence: One TypeScript service. The REST and WebSocket sync roles share an image
scores.rationale: Starts with the simplest workable topology on proven libraries, defers multi-region, E2EE, SSO and search with explicit triggers, while omitting nothing essential for real-time co-editing.

scores.evidence: V1 fails → server decides edit order with operational transforms (ShareDB), and Phase 1 is re-planned
scores.rationale: Dependency-justified phase order, a concrete Phase 0 slice, specific technology and schema decisions, checkable exit criteria per phase, and pre-stated fallbacks if gates fail let a team start immediately.

checklist.evidence: CRDT (Yjs + y-prosemirror)... V1 fails → server decides edit order with operational transforms (ShareDB)
Freeze content schema v1 and the sync protocol, both versioned, with the min-version handshake
random schema-valid edits, with messages reordered, duplicated and delayed... 0 divergent copies over 10k sessions and 1M edits
Confirm only after the Postgres commit... It writes a snapshot, checks it matches a full replay of the log
Redis pub/sub between replicas... reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter... Autoscaling and load shedding
Client offline queue in IndexedDB that resends unconfirmed edits; reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter
checked on the server: on WebSocket connect, on every incoming edit... Revocation ends live sessions
Per-user undo and redo (Yjs UndoManager)... Version-history UI built on the snapshots
Presence and cursors (Yjs awareness; temporary, never stored)
Phase 1: Document contracts (the stored format, sync protocol and permission model have the widest rework if wrong)
~1 MB text with 100k edits of history loads ≤1 s, ≤50 MB memory... 50 editors per document, each typing 5 edits/s
clients below the minimum schema version are rejected at connect... Old and new clients (v1, and a v2 with a new node type)

traps.evidence: Every copy ends up identical without the server deciding order
Self-host open-source Yjs, Hocuspocus and TipTap
An internal user types one character into a document in browser A. It shows up in browser B... connected to the *other* server replica
Confirm only after the Postgres commit, using a managed HA database with synchronous replication
Yjs merges correctly on our content schema and is fast enough at our document sizes

note: An exceptionally rigorous, correctly grounded plan that validates convergence and durability before lock-in; only soft spots are rich-text merge semantics detail, restore-while-editing behavior, and cost estimation depth.
